# Atrioventricular block

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Internal medicine > Cardiology and angiology > Arrhythmias > Atrioventricular block*

[Original Article Link](/library/I50Ylg)

---

## Summary

Atrioventricular block (AV block) is characterized by an interrupted or delayed conduction between the <u>atria</u> and the ventricles. There are three degrees of AV block, categorized according to the extent of the delay or interruption. First-degree blocks are identifiable on <u>ECG</u> by a prolonged <u>PR interval</u>. <u>Second-degree AV blocks</u> are further divided into four subtypes: <u>Mobitz type I</u> (also called Wenckebach), <u>Mobitz type II</u>, <u>2:1 AV block</u>, and <u>high-grade AV block</u>. In <u>Mobitz type I</u> blocks, a progressive prolongation of the <u>PR interval</u> culminates in a nonconducted <u>P wave</u> (“dropped beat”). <u>Mobitz type II</u> blocks generate dropped <u>QRS complexes</u> at regular intervals (e.g., 3:2, 4:3, or 5:4), often leading to <u>bradycardia</u>. A <u>2:1 AV block</u> has a regular pattern in which every second atrial impulse is not conducted to the ventricles. In second-degree <u>high-grade AV block</u>, two or more consecutive <u>P waves</u> do not generate a ventricular response. A <u>third-degree AV block</u>, also known as <u>complete heart block</u>, involves the total interruption of the electrical impulse between the <u>atria</u> and ventricles. The complete absence of conduction results in a <u>ventricular escape rhythm</u>, whose rate depends on the level at which the <u>escape rhythm</u> is generated. AV blocks may be asymptomatic or cause <u>symptoms of bradycardia</u>. Depending on the <u>heart rate</u>, symptoms can be severe and include <u>heart failure</u> or <u>syncope</u>. Asymptomatic patients with first-degree and <u>Mobitz type I</u> blocks usually only require observation, whereas higher-degree blocks necessitate <u>permanent pacemaker</u> insertion.

## Etiology

See also “<u>Causes of bradycardia</u>.”




| <br>Etiology of atrioventricular blocks <br> |  |
| --- | --- |
| Category | <br>Examples  [[2]](/library/ntY7VI) |
| <u>Structural heart disease</u> | <br><br>* <u>Ischemic heart disease</u><br><br>* Acute <u>MI</u>  [[4]](/library/OhbIVt)<br><br>* Chronic <u>ischemic cardiomyopathy</u><br><br>* <u>Congenital heart disease</u> and congenital <u>third-degree AV block</u><br><br>* Post-cardiac intervention: e.g., <u>surgery</u> (particularly involving valves), ablations, or <u>TAVI</u><br><br>* Inflammatory/<u>infiltrative cardiomyopathy</u>: e.g., <u>myocarditis</u>, <u>amyloidosis</u>, <u>sarcoidosis</u>, <u>autoimmune connective tissue disorders</u>, <u>lymphoma</u>  [[5]](/library/RNbla8)<br><br>* Degenerative: <u>idiopathic</u> <u>fibrosis</u> of the <u>conduction system</u> (Lenègre-Lev syndrome) causing <u>RBBB</u> and eventually AV block<br><br><br> |
| Neurocardiogenic | <br>* Increased <u>vagal</u> tone: can be physiological or pathological<br><br>* Healthy individuals with high levels of exercise (e.g., in professional athletes): most often transient <u>1° AV block</u> and <u>Mobitz I</u> [[6]](/library/iqXJy_)<br><br>* <u>Obstructive sleep apnea</u><br><br>* During <u>vomiting</u>, suctioning, or <u>intubation</u> [[7]](/library/qdbCIs)<br><br> |
| Toxic/metabolic | <br><br>* <u>Electrolyte</u> disorders: e.g., <u>hyperkalemia</u><br><br>* <u>Acid-base disorders</u><br><br>* Cardiotoxic drugs: e.g., <u>beta blockers</u>, <u>calcium channel blockers</u>, or <u>digoxin</u> (therapeutic doses or overdoses)<br><br>* Other toxicity: e.g., <u>carbon monoxide</u>, <u>cyanide</u><br><br><br> |
| Infectious | <br><br>* Bacterial <u>endocarditis</u><br><br>* <u>Lyme carditis</u><br><br>* <u>Acute rheumatic fever</u><br><br><br> |
| Endocrine | <br><br>* <u>Thyroid disease</u><br><br>* <u>Adrenal</u> disease<br><br><br> |
| Neuromuscular | <br>* <u>Myotonic dystrophy</u><br><br> |

## Clinical features

* Asymptomatic (common): especially with first-degree and <u>Mobitz type I</u> blocks [[2]](/library/ntY7VI)

* <u>Clinical features of end-organ hypoperfusion</u> (due to <u>bradycardia</u>) may be present, including: [[9]](/library/jNb_a8)

* Fatigue

* Exercise intolerance

* <u>Dyspnea</u>

* <u>Dizziness</u>

* <u>Syncope</u>

* Irregular rhythms (e.g., <u>Mobitz I</u>): <u>palpitations</u>

* Loss of atrioventricular synchrony (e.g., extreme <u>1° AV block</u> or <u>3° AV block</u>) : [[2]](/library/ntY7VI)

* Feeling of pulsations in the neck or chest

* Cannon A waves: <u>physical examination</u> finding seen in <u>AV dissociation</u> (e.g., in <u>third-degree heart block</u>)

* Caused by the <u>atria</u> and ventricles contracting simultaneously, which leads to blood being pushed against a closed <u>tricuspid valve</u>

* The result is a retrograde pressure wave throughout the venous system that may appear as pulsations in the jugular <u>vein</u>.

* <u>Symptoms of heart failure</u>  [[2]](/library/ntY7VI)

* Significant pauses of <u>asystole</u>

* Stokes-Adams attacks [[10]](/library/0VbeGs)

* Sudden losses of consciousness that may occur with brief <u>prodromal</u> symptoms, e.g., <u>dizziness</u>, or without any warning, usually lasting a few seconds

* Attacks are caused by ventricular <u>asystole</u>, most commonly due to <u>third-degree heart block</u>, especially <u>idiopathic</u> <u>paroxysmal</u> AV block.

* <u>Cardiac arrest</u>

---

## First-degree AV block

* Description [[2]](/library/ntY7VI)

* <u>PR interval</u> > 200 ms

* No interruption in atrial to ventricular conduction

* Rate of <u>SA node</u> = <u>heart rate</u>

* Often discovered incidentally on <u>ECG</u>

* Risk of progression to <u>complete heart block</u>: low, as the block results from slowed conduction through the <u>AV node</u> [[2]](/library/ntY7VI)

## Second-degree AV block

### Mobitz type I (Wenckebach) [[2]](/library/ntY7VI)




* Description

* Progressive lengthening of the <u>PR interval</u> until a beat is dropped, which means a regular atrial impulse does not reach the ventricles (a normal <u>P wave</u> is not followed by a <u>QRS complex</u>)

* Mostly regular rhythm separated by short pauses, which may lead to <u>bradycardia</u> (<u>regularly irregular rhythm</u>)

* Rate of <u>SA node</u> > <u>heart</u> rate

* Risk of progression to <u>complete heart block</u>: typically low, as the block is most often at the level of the <u>AV node</u>





![Second-degree atrioventricular block](media/laj0wl2kc0ittvo7q1jcv1rz.jpg)

Second-degree atrioventricular block

![Second-degree atrioventricular block: Mobitz I/Wenckebach](media/v89kdpxue72v9qgcr58yazn1.jpg)

Second-degree atrioventricular block: Mobitz I/Wenckebach




> [!NOTE]
> First-degree and <u>Mobitz type I</u> second-degree AV blocks may be seen in healthy individuals, e.g., in athletes with increased <u>vagal</u> tone. Patients are often asymptomatic.




### Mobitz type II [[2]](/library/ntY7VI)




* Description

* Single or intermittent nonconducted <u>P waves</u> without <u>QRS complexes</u>

* The <u>PR interval</u> remains constant.

* The conduction of atrial impulses to the ventricles typically follows a regular pattern, e.g.: [[2]](/library/ntY7VI)

* 3:2 block: regular AV block with 3 atrial depolarizations but only 2 atrial impulses that reach the ventricles (<u>heart rate</u> = ⅔ <u>SA node</u> rate)

* 4:3 block: regular AV block with 4 atrial depolarizations but only 3 atrial impulses that reach the ventricles (<u>heart rate</u> = ¾ <u>SA node</u> rate)

* While 2:1 block follows a regular pattern, it cannot be classified as <u>Mobitz type I</u> or II and is classified separately (see “<u>2:1 AV block</u>”). [[2]](/library/ntY7VI)

* Risk of progression to <u>complete heart block</u>: high (> 50%), as it is typically due to <u>infranodal block</u> (usually in the <u>His-Purkinje system</u>) [[7]](/library/qdbCIs)





![Mobitz type II second-degree atrioventricular block and bifascicular block](media/ow80qtpqjzax70a3sftff65u.jpg)

Mobitz type II second-degree atrioventricular block and bifascicular block




> [!TIP]
> <u>Mobitz type II</u> block can progress to <u>third-degree heart block</u>; therefore, all patients should be admitted for <u>continuous cardiac monitoring</u> and treatment.




### Other variants




#### 2:1 AV block [[2]](/library/ntY7VI)




* Description

* Inhibited conduction of every second atrial <u>depolarization</u> (<u>P wave</u>) to the ventricles (<u>heart</u> rate = ½ SA node rate)

* Cannot be classified as <u>Mobitz I</u> or <u>Mobitz II</u> as only one <u>PR interval</u> is observed before the subsequent dropped complex

* Often a transient rhythm occurring on a baseline <u>Mobitz I</u> or <u>Mobitz II</u> rhythm

* Risk of progression to <u>complete heart block</u>: depends on level of block 

* Block at the level of the <u>AV node</u> (more common): low

* <u>Infranodal block</u> (less common): high





![2:1 second-degree atrioventricular block and right bundle branch block](media/fjnyesuyxhddkd1ft7e9826r.jpg)

2:1 second-degree atrioventricular block and right bundle branch block

![Second degree AV block (2:1)](media/yiyzqxdw1j3u34yfbzxf60bk.jpg)

Second degree AV block (2:1)

![Second degree AV block (2:1)](media/mtwjwrjj0pa1haajgcwxgbm5.jpg)

Second degree AV block (2:1)




#### High-grade AV block [[2]](/library/ntY7VI)[[7]](/library/qdbCIs)




* Description

* A block in which ≥ 2 consecutive <u>P waves</u> do not generate a ventricular response, e.g., 3:1 block

* As some <u>P waves</u> do generate a ventricular response, <u>high-grade AV block</u> differs from <u>third-degree heart block</u> in which there is complete dissociation.

* Risk of progression to <u>complete heart block</u>: typically high, but depends on duration and reversibility of block

---

## Third-degree AV block (complete heart block)

* Description

* Third-degree AV block is a complete block with no conduction between the <u>atria</u> and ventricles.

* <u>P waves</u> and <u>QRS complexes</u> have their own regular rhythm but bear no relationship to each other (<u>AV dissociation</u>).

* Risk of progression to <u>cardiogenic shock</u> or <u>cardiac arrest</u>: : High; Sudden onset <u>3° AV block</u> can result in ventricular <u>asystole</u>, which lasts until an <u>escape rhythm</u> takes over.

* <u>Escape rhythms</u>: can be generated by sites that are usually located near the <u>AV node</u> or near the <u>bundle of His</u>.

* Ventricular escape rhythm [[11]](/library/1Vb2ts)

* A rhythm generated at the level of the <u>bundle of His</u>

* <u>Heart rate</u> 20–40/minute

* <u>Wide QRS complexes</u>

* Junctional escape rhythm  [[11]](/library/1Vb2ts)

* A rhythm generated at the level of the <u>AV node</u>

* <u>Heart rate</u> 40–60/minute

* <u>Narrow QRS complexes</u>

* <u>Idiopathic</u> <u>paroxysmal</u> AV block [[12]](/library/WVbPts)

* A subtype of <u>third-degree AV block</u> that can affect patients with otherwise normal AV conduction.

* Recurrent episodes may lead to <u>Stokes-Adams attacks</u>.

## Management of AV blocks

### Approach



* All patients

* Obtain 12-lead <u>ECG</u> immediately (with or without <u>rhythm strip</u>) to ascertain the type of AV block.

* Evaluate for <u>signs of unstable bradycardia</u> and apply <u>transcutaneous pacing</u> pads if required.




| <br>Management approach to patients with AV block [[2]](/library/ntY7VI)<br> |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
|  | Low-risk AV block | <br>High-risk AV block<br> |
| Type of AV block | <br><br>* <u>1° AV block</u><br><br>* <u>Mobitz I</u><br><br>* <u>2:1 AV block</u> thought to be at the <u>AV nodal</u> level<br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Mobitz II</u><br><br>* <u>2:1 AV block</u> due to <u>infranodal block</u><br><br>* <u>High-grade AV block</u><br><br>* <u>3° AV block</u><br><br><br> |
| Unstable patients | <br><br>* Interventions include: <u>atropine</u>, <u>transvenous pacing</u>, <u>transcutaneous pacing</u>, <u>inotropic</u> medication (e.g., IV <u>epinephrine</u>)<br><br>* See “<u>Unstable bradycardia</u>” for the management algorithm.<br><br>* Continue investigations and definitive management once the patient is stabilized.<br><br><br> |  |
| Stable patients | <br>* Identify and treat the underlying cause (e.g., <u>structural heart disease</u>, <u>digoxin toxicity</u>).<br><br>* Check serum <u>electrolytes</u> and provide <u>electrolyte repletion</u> as needed.<br><br>* Screen for and treat <u>acute coronary syndrome</u> in patients with <u>atherosclerotic risk factors</u> (e.g., serial <u>ECG</u>, <u>troponin</u>, <u>aspirin</u>).<br><br>* Further diagnostics and specific management according to suspected <u>etiology of AV block</u><br><br> |  |
| <br>* Consider <u>cardiac imaging</u> (e.g., <u>TTE</u>) if no clear etiology and suspected <u>structural heart disease</u><br><br> | <br>* Obtain <u>cardiac imaging</u> on all patients<br><br>* Preferred initial test: <u>TTE</u><br><br>* Consider advanced <u>cardiac imaging</u>, e.g., <u>MRI</u>, CT, or <u>TEE</u><br><br> |  |
| <br><br>* Typically no specific treatment if asymptomatic and no <u>infranodal block</u><br><br>* Outpatient screening for <u>infranodal block</u> and monitoring for progression<br><br>* See “<u>Management of low-risk AV block</u>.”<br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Continuous cardiac monitoring</u><br><br>* Admission for <u>temporary pacing</u><br><br>* <u>Permanent pacemaker</u> for all patients with irreversible blocks<br><br>* See “<u>Management of high-risk AV block</u>.”<br><br><br> |  |





![Management of bradycardia](media/f100mb6a6t1xitj3yfnldy7x.jpg)

Management of bradycardia




### Evaluation of underlying causes [[2]](/library/ntY7VI)[[13]](/library/0rXefz)




* Order <u>laboratory studies</u> based on suspected etiology, e.g.:

* <u>Renal function tests</u>

* <u>Liver chemistries</u>

* <u>Troponin</u>

* <u>Antibody</u> <u>titer</u>, e.g. for <u>Lyme disease</u>

* <u>Electrolytes</u> (including <u>potassium</u>)

* <u>Blood gas</u> (serum <u>pH</u>)

* <u>TSH</u>

* Identify medications that can impair AV conduction. 

* <u>Beta-blockers</u>

* <u>Non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers</u>

* <u>Digoxin</u>

* Others: <u>clonidine</u>, <u>amiodarone</u>, <u>adenosine</u>, <u>flecainide</u>, <u>class IB antiarrhythmics</u>, and some <u>antidepressants</u>.

* Consider measuring drug levels: e.g. <u>digoxin</u> level





### Management of low-risk AV block [[2]](/library/ntY7VI)



* Patients on medication that can cause or exacerbate AV conduction

* Monitor for progression with periodic <u>ECGs</u>.

* Discontinue if patients have other preexisting conduction abnormalities. [[13]](/library/0rXefz)




#### Indications for pacemaker placement [[2]](/library/ntY7VI)




Patients with an irreversible AV block and the following:




* <u>Infranodal block</u>

* Patients with <u>infranodal block</u> should be treated as high-grade AV blocks

* If the level of the AV block is unclear, assess with [[2]](/library/ntY7VI)[[7]](/library/qdbCIs)

* <u>Exercise ECG</u>

* Electrophysiologic study

* <u>Carotid sinus massage</u> or pharmacological challenge

* Neuromuscular disease associated with AV block (known or suspected): refer to a specialist for possible pacemaker.

* Certain symptomatic patients
* Assess for <u>correlation</u> of symptoms using an ambulatory <u>Holter monitor</u>.

* Permanent pacing is indicated if symptoms clearly correlate with AV block.

* If symptoms do not correlate, continue monitoring as an outpatient





### Management of high-risk AV block [[2]](/library/ntY7VI)[[13]](/library/0rXefz)




* Potentially reversible cause

* Consider <u>temporary pacing</u>.

* Adapt management depending on the suspected underlying cause

* Manage <u>medication-induced bradycardia</u>, e.g., <u>beta blocker toxicity</u>, <u>digoxin toxicity</u>, <u>CCB toxicity</u>

* Perform <u>PCI</u> and avoid early pacemaker implantation < 72 h in patients with AV block caused by acute <u>MI</u>.

* See “Special situations” in “<u>Unstable bradycardia</u>” for other patient groups (e.g., <u>cardiac transplant</u>).

* <u>Permanent pacemaker</u> placement is indicated if:

* AV block persists despite adequate treatment

* Medication causing AV block is necessary and not replaceable

* Irreversible cause

* All patients with Mobitz Type II, high-grade, or <u>third-degree AV block</u> require the placement of a <u>permanent pacemaker</u>.

* Consider a <u>defibrillator</u> if the AV block is caused by infiltrative processes or neuromuscular disease with conduction block.
